Helping little readers
find their way.

Making foundational literacy more intuitive, accessible, and fun for K–2 learners.

ProjectEVERFI · WORD Force
My roleProduct · UX · UI

The challenge: keeping young readers engaged

WORD Force is a 15-game literacy adventure for K–2 learners. The original desktop experience launched in 2020, but engagement dropped steeply after the first few games. Feedback and testing showed that younger children struggled with navigation, game interactions, and mouse controls.

For version 2.0, our goal was to make the experience easier to understand and more engaging, while introducing literacy interventions and tutorial videos to support struggling readers.

My role: connecting research and product design

I worked across product design, UX, and UI: remapping learning flows, simplifying interactions, refining interfaces, and directing usability testing. I collaborated with project management, UX research, product leads, visual designers, learning experience design, and development.

The 2022 project brought together six months of collaborative work. My tools included Figma, Trymata, and Dovetail.

Research designed for children

Most testing platforms require adult participants, so we adapted our approach. We recruited guardians of children ages 4–7 through Trymata for unmoderated sessions with screen and audio recordings.

I ran more than 20 tests, reviewed over 100 session videos, and wrote detailed research summaries. For each game, I documented where children stayed engaged, where they struggled, and which patterns appeared across participants. I also ran A/B comparisons between versions 1.0 and 2.0 to assess progress.

Turning findings into design changes

A clearer path through the learning

I remapped the overall game flow to connect lessons, mini-games, and interventions. The challenge was deciding where learning support belonged so it helped children without disrupting the experience.

Simpler interactions for younger learners

Feedback from the original version and observations from testing showed that navigation and interactions were difficult for younger children. We simplified those interactions and refined the interfaces to make controls more intuitive, age-appropriate, and consistent across games.

Shared components across 15 games

The design team expanded the component library with streamlined assets and standardized colors, sizing, icons, and typography. This gave the games a more coherent visual language and a reusable foundation for future updates.

Launch and outcomes

WORD Force 2.0 launched after six months of collaboration. The project’s reported outcomes included longer play and more return visits, clearer understanding of how to play, easier mouse controls for younger children, and improved comprehension through interventions and tutorial videos.

These are qualitative outcomes reported in the original case study; numerical improvement rates are not available here.

What I learned

Designing for children requires flexibility in both research and interface design. Testing highlighted how much accessibility needs can vary between ages 4 and 7—even within a one-year age gap. Details such as animation pacing and button size can materially affect a child’s experience.

The project strengthened my approach to adapting research methods for young audiences and using repeated observation to guide design decisions.
